cim: Letters: Deltgen on Artificial Intelligence; Angelucci Says Chowan County Must Close Data Center Loopholes
cim_eredeti: Letters: Deltgen on Artificial Intelligence; Angelucci Says Chowan County Must Close Data Center Loopholes
szoveg_eredeti:
Two letters — one from Florian Deltgen about AI and another from Joe Angelucci about data centers in Chowan County. Both are very smart guys!

In a Commissioner Meeting of the Pitt County Commission on Monday, November 16, 2026, the Commission majority voted to put a moratorium on the construction of an AI data center in Pitt County. This means that for another two years nothing will happen.

This is a small contribution to help China increase its chances to control the AI market and systems in the USA. Not that I am totally happy about AI. I see major risks in this new technology for our individual liberty and national sovereignty. China already supplies major portions of the materials, components, and manufacturing capacity for solar panels, for wind turbines, and for key infrastructure elements of AI data centers as well as significant elements of our power, energy storage, and networking gear in data centers.

China dominates nearly the entire photovoltaic supply chain:

Additional elements such as solar glass, aluminum frames, encapsulants, and a large share of inverters and silver paste also come from China.

China is the world’s largest manufacturer of complete wind turbines and many key parts thereof, such as:

Rare-earth permanent magnets, and steel and specialized alloys for towers and structural components; and China holds the largest global manufacturing capacity for blades, nacelles, gearboxes, generators, and towers for wind turbines.

China also supplies substantial shares of the supporting infrastructure:

Transformers and switchgear, batteries and energy storage / UPS systems, optical modules, transceivers for high-speed networking inside data centers, cooling equipment, printed circuit boards, electrical steel, copper-related materials, and various chemicals and critical minerals.

China is also a net exporter of much of the infrastructure side of AI data centers, such as power gear, batteries, optics, or cooling technology.

In short: Solar panels are overwhelmingly Chinese-made across almost every stage, wind turbines rely heavily on Chinese rare-earth magnets and large-scale component manufacturing, and AI data centers depend on Chinese supply for power transformation, energy storage, and high-speed optical networking far more than for the core AI chips themselves.

However, building an AI data center makes little sense without simultaneously providing the necessary power supply. A representative modern large AI-focused data center needs on the order of 100–500 MW of electrical capacity, with rack densities of ~120 kW. Exact requirements depend on the GPU generation, utilization rate, cooling efficiency, and whether the site is optimized purely for AI training/inference.

Pitt Co. planning staff identified gaps in the existing rules for large-scale data processing facilities, defined as facilities on one or more acres. These include a lack of standards for electrical load/infrastructure, water use, low-frequency noise, air quality from generators, and differentiation between small facilities and large/hyperscale campuses.

Staff noted that some projects elsewhere involve 500-acre campuses with hundreds of megawatts of demand, and that the current ordinance does not adequately address scale differences or cumulative impacts.

The move followed resident concerns about electricity and water consumption, potential rate increases, noise, environmental effects, and the county’s ability to regulate such facilities. It is apparently intended as a temporary pause, not a permanent ban, and can end earlier if new rules are adopted. This two-year delay follows an earlier one-year delay that was caused by similar concerns. Note that the issue of where the electrical power would come from that is needed to run the AI Data Center was not among the citizens’ or county staff’s concerns. If you want an AI data center, you must first create the power supply structure for it. If you are serious about starting the construction of an AI Data Center in 2028, you should be working on creating the power supply system now!

One wonders, what has been accomplished during the one-year delay? Have any of these largely administrative (not to say bureaucratic) concerns been remedied? If not or only a few, what guaranties do we have that they will be remedied come the end of 2028? Don’t put off until tomorrow what you can do today. Because the clock is ticking.

By delaying AI data center construction, we are further supporting China’s lead in AI technology and our dependence on it. Yes, it all costs money. But falling behind in the race for leadership in the AI technology market will make us a second-class nation and cement our dependence on our strategic adversary, China, for all time to come. In addition, an AI facility could generate a significant income for the county.

Let’s face it: Once something has been invented it cannot be disinvented. Like it or hate it, we are stuck with AI. To oppose AI today is like opposing motorized flight in 1903. The best we can do is to become the leader in this field, end our dangerous dependence on Chinese technology both in the field of AI and of power generation, and make laws and regulations that mitigate the potential negative effects of AI on our personal lives and our nation to a tolerable level. We need to make haste to resolve the problems, real or perceived, associated with AI technology in Pitt County and build a power supply system and the AI Data Center ASAP. Simply waiting yet another two years is the worst of all responses. It’s like a football game in which one team takes a 3-minute break, while the other team keeps on playing. Guess, which team will win!

Florian Deltgen is a resident of Tyrrell County.

While the Town of Edenton recently decided to table its UDO changes regarding data centers for additional review, Chowan County faces an invisible and immediate regulatory emergency now.

Currently, Chowan County’s land-use codes do not define or list “data centers” anywhere. Because of this omission, an industrial-scale data center facility could legally bypass the public entirely, securing staff-level administrative approval without a single public hearing or a vote by our county commissioners.

Unchecked data centers bring massive infrastructure headaches: immense strains on our local electric grid, heavy demands on our water resources, and continuous noise pollution from industrial cooling systems.

Our regional neighbors—Camden, Gates, and Pasquotank counties—have already hit the pause button by passing active moratoria to rewrite their zoning laws. Because we have no protections on the books, Chowan County is now the unprotected path of least resistance for developers looking to exploit regional loopholes.

Our Chowan County Commissioners must act quickly to pass a temporary, flexible 18 -month moratorium on all data centers. This isn’t about stopping growth—it’s about a strategic pause to work alongside Edenton and establish unified rules that protect our citizen’s utility rates, property values, and rural heritage. If we don’t look before we leap, we risk losing control over our infrastructure.
